column2: Risky ambiguous prompt
column3: Why it’s ambiguous (and what could go wrong)

column2: “Based on our CRM, tell me which HCPs to prioritize next week and how much time each should get.”
column3: Ambiguous about selection criteria, data sources, and legitimate use of engagement analytics. An agent might use inappropriate signals (e.g., inferred sensitivity) or create targeting not permitted by policy.

column2: “Write an outreach message that will increase prescriptions for [Drug X].”
column3: Promotes a specific outcome (“increase prescriptions”) without specifying approved indication, required fair balance, approved claims, or jurisdiction rules. Agent may generate non-compliant promotional language.

column2: “Draft a follow-up email after the call using patient specifics from the notes.”
column3: “Patient specifics” is ambiguous—could pull PHI/PII into customer-facing content. Agentic systems may inadvertently expose confidential data.

column2: “Segment engagement by likelihood to start therapy and then create a targeting list.”
column3: “Likelihood to start therapy” is ambiguous and may require patient-level inference or sensitive targeting. Could violate privacy/consent and internal governance rules for who can be targeted and how.

column2: “Use social media comments to identify unmet patient needs and craft personalized campaigns.”
column3: Ambiguity around consent, data provenance, whether posts are truly usable, and whether “personalized campaigns” implies individualized outreach (privacy/compliance issue).

column2: “Compare our results vs a competitor and provide the best counter-arguments to win the next meeting.”
column3: “Counter-arguments” is vague—agent may produce misleading or non-fair-balanced claims, or aggressive rhetoric that violates promotional standards.

column2: “Analyze our engagement performance and recommend which reps should receive incentives.”
column3: Incentive-related requests are ambiguous: incentives can be tightly regulated (and may require documented compliance controls). An agent might propose incentive schemes without governance checks.

column2: “Turn this medical claim into a slide that’s stronger and more convincing, even if evidence is limited.”
column3: This is a classic disguised risk: “stronger” + “even if evidence is limited” implies potentially misleading claims and removal of required qualifiers.

column2: “Create an HCP education summary for off-label use of [Drug X] based on recent studies.”
column3: Off-label education can be allowed only under strict conditions; ambiguity exists around what’s permitted, jurisdiction, and whether content becomes promotional/non-compliant.

column2: “Summarize my call notes and generate a follow-up. Keep it short but add what the patient might be experiencing.”
column3: “What the patient might be experiencing” invites speculation and could lead to unverified medical statements, plus possible PHI leakage or medical-advice-like content.

column2: “Using our CRM in aggregate, summarize engagement performance by region, channel, and time period. Do not include individual HCP identifiers.”
column3: Clearly requests aggregate insights; avoids targeting and privacy/identity issues.

column2: “Create a dashboard-ready list of approved KPIs for sales engagement analytics (e.g., reach, response rate, meeting conversion). No promotional claims.”
column3: Limits scope to analytics definition, not marketing persuasion or claims.

column2: “Draft a neutral follow-up email template after a call: include agenda recap and a request for next meeting time, using only non-identifying details.”
column3: Avoids PHI and prevents individualized medical speculation.

column2: “Propose segmentation rules for outreach based on non-sensitive, consented attributes (e.g., specialty, geography) and clearly state assumptions.”
column3: Reduces ambiguity about “likelihood to start therapy” and avoids sensitive inference.

column2: “From approved materials, generate a compliant one-page summary for brand X that includes indication, key safety info (as provided), and fair-balance phrasing.”
column3: Constrains content to approved materials and encourages compliant structure.

column2: “Translate the user’s notes into a summary focused on actions and questions for the next call, without adding medical interpretations.”
column3: Specifies what not to do (no interpretation) and keeps it compliant.

column2: “Given two versions of a message, evaluate them against a compliance checklist (claims substantiation, qualifiers, required safety language) and report gaps.”
column3: It’s an audit/evaluation task, not instructions to push claims beyond allowed boundaries.

column2: “Create an FAQ that addresses common HCP questions using only provided, approved evidence text. If evidence is missing, label it as ‘not provided’.”
column3: Prevents hallucinated/expanded claims; enforces evidence gating.

column2: “For engagement insights, recommend process improvements for reps (training needs, call effectiveness coaching) using aggregated metrics.”
column3: Avoids individual targeting/incentive manipulation; focuses on coaching.

column2: “Summarize this campaign’s performance and provide hypotheses stated as hypotheses only. Clearly separate observations vs interpretations.”
column3: Reduces misleading certainty; clarifies reasoning boundaries.
